The Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) score in Express Entry is calculated based on several factors, including:

- Skills
- Education
- Language ability
- Work experience
- Other factors

The CRS is a points-based system used to assess and score your profile and rank it in the Express Entry pool. The maximum score is 1,200 points. To get an invitation to apply, your CRS score must be above the minimum points score of your round of invitations (Source: Express Entry: Check your score, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/check-score.html).

For more detailed information on how points are calculated, you can refer to the full CRS criteria (Source: Express Entry: Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) criteria, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/check-score/crs-criteria.html).

The Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) score in Express Entry is calculated based on several factors, including:

1. **Core Human Capital Factors**: Age, education, work experience, and official language proficiency.
2. **Skill Transferability Factors**: Education, foreign work experience, and certificate of qualification in combination with other factors.
3. **Additional Points**: For factors such as Canadian work experience, a valid job offer, a provincial nomination, a sibling in Canada, and French language proficiency.

For example, under Skill Transferability factors, you can earn points for:
- Having a post-secondary degree and good/strong official languages proficiency (up to 50 points).
- Having foreign work experience and good/strong official languages proficiency (up to 50 points).
- Having a certificate of qualification in a trade occupation and good/strong official languages proficiency (up to 50 points).

Additionally, you can earn points for Canadian work experience, ranging from 0 to 80 points depending on the duration of your work experience.

(Source: Express Entry: Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) criteria, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/check-score/crs-criteria.html)

To enter more than one educational credential in your Express Entry profile, follow these steps:

- Go to the Study and languages form in your profile.
- Fill in all the fields in the Education history section with your first credential.
- Use the credential for your highest degree, diploma or certificate.
- Click Save and add. The fields you just filled out will go blank.
- Your credential will appear in the Education history table below the Save and add button. Repeat steps 1 to 3 for all your remaining educational credentials.
You can’t submit more than 1 educational credential in the same field. (Source: Educational credential assessment, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/documents/education-assessment.html)

A certified translator is a member in good standing of a professional translation association in Canada or abroad. Their certification must be confirmed by a seal or stamp that shows the translator’s membership number. Any family member, representative or consultant of the applicant who may be a lawyer, notary or translator is not permitted to translate documents. A translator in the process of receiving their certification or accreditation is not considered a certified translator for IRCC’s purposes. (Source: Apply for permanent residence through Express Entry, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/apply-permanent-residence.html)

A certified translator is a member in good standing of a provincial or territorial organization of translators and interpreters in Canada. The translator will seal or stamp the translated document, and the seal or stamp will have a membership number that can be verified. (Source: Canadian citizenship for Stateless people: Get the forms and documents, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/stateless/forms-documents.html)

Category-based selection in the Express Entry program invites candidates who meet specific criteria related to economic goals. Here's how it works:

1. **Category Selection**: Categories are chosen based on labour market needs and input from partners. Examples include French-language proficiency, healthcare occupations, STEM occupations, and more (Source: Express Entry: Category-based selection, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/rounds-invitations/category-based-selection.html).

2. **Profile Creation**: Candidates create an online Express Entry profile in their IRCC secure account (Source: Express Entry: Category-based selection, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/rounds-invitations/category-based-selection.html).

3. **Pool Placement**: If eligible for one of the Express Entry programs, candidates are placed in the Express Entry pool (Source: Express Entry: Category-based selection, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/rounds-invitations/category-based-selection.html).

4. **CRS Score**: Candidates are assigned a Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) score based on their profile (Source: Express Entry: Category-based selection, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/rounds-invitations/category-based-selection.html).

5. **Category Eligibility**: Candidates are identified based on their profile for eligibility in a specific category (Source: Express Entry: Category-based selection, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/rounds-invitations/category-based-selection.html).

6. **Invitation to Apply**: Eligible candidates with the highest CRS scores are invited to apply for permanent residence (Source: Express Entry: Category-based selection, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/rounds-invitations/category-based-selection.html).

- The employer didn't put in enough effort to make sure the workplace was free of any of the following: physical abuse, sexual abuse, psychological abuse, financial abuse, reprisal. (Source: Employers who have been found non-compliant, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/employers-non-compliant.html)

Penalties for non-compliance under the International Mobility Program include:

- Warning letters
- Monetary penalties from $500 to $100,000 per violation, up to a maximum of $1 million over 1 year
- A ban from hiring temporary workers through the Temporary Foreign Worker Program or the International Mobility Program for 1, 2, 5, or 10 years
- A permanent ban from hiring temporary workers through the Temporary Foreign Worker Program or the International Mobility Program (for serious violations only)
- Refusal of any pending work permit applications tied to your business
- Revocation of active work permits that are tied to your business
- Addition to the public list of employers who have been non-compliant if you receive a monetary penalty of any amount or a ban of any length of time

(Source: Penalties under the International Mobility Program, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/hire-temporary-foreign/international-mobility-program/penalties.html)

To request faster processing of your work permit extension if you need to travel urgently, you need to provide the following documents:

- Proof of urgency (one or more of the following):
  - A letter from your employer explaining why the travel is urgent and the impact on jobs or the success of the business
  - A death certificate
  - Evidence of serious illness (for example, a doctor’s note)

- Proof of travel due to the emergency:
  - A copy of your plane, bus, train, or boat ticket, OR
  - Proof of payment and the itinerary (if you don’t have your ticket yet)

All documents must be in either English or French. If they’re in another language, you must provide a certified translation. (Source: How to request faster processing of your work permit extension if you need to travel urgently, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/extend/travel-outside-canada/faster-processing.html)

Yes, you can participate in the International Co-op (Internship) program if you meet the following criteria:

- You are an Estonian citizen.
- You have a valid Estonian passport for the duration of your stay in Canada.
- You are between the ages of 18 and 35 (inclusive).
- You are enrolled at a post-secondary institution in Estonia and must be registered students for the duration of the internship.
- You want to complete a work placement or internship in Canada to fulfil part of your academic curriculum (up to 12 months).
- You have a signed letter of offer or a signed contract of employment before submitting your profile to the pool.

Aby złożyć wniosek o eTA na przyjazd do Kanady, należy postępować zgodnie z poniższymi krokami:

1. Przygotuj swój paszport, kartę kredytową oraz adres email.
2. Złóż wniosek online na oficjalnej stronie internetowej Rządu Kanady.
3. Wypełnij formularz, odpowiadając na kilka pytań.
4. Dokonaj płatności w wysokości 7 dolarów kanadyjskich za jedną osobę.
5. Otrzymasz potwierdzenie złożenia wniosku drogą emailową, zazwyczaj w ciągu kilku minut.

Pamiętaj, że nie można zachować wypełnionego formularza, dlatego przygotuj wszystkie potrzebne informacje przed rozpoczęciem wniosku. (Source: Złóż wniosek o Elektroniczną Autoryzację Podróży (eTA), https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/visit-canada/eta/apply-pl.html)

Aby złożyć wniosek o eTA na przyjazd do Kanady, postępuj zgodnie z poniższymi krokami:

1. Przygotuj swój ważny paszport, kartę kredytową lub debitową oraz przeczytaj instrukcje.
2. Złóż wniosek korzystając z formularza internetowego. Formularz nie może być zachowany, więc przygotuj swoje informacje z góry.
3. Dokonaj płatności CAD 7$ za swoją eTA tuż po wypełnieniu wniosku.
4. Otrzymasz potwierdzenie złożenia wniosku o eTA pocztą elektroniczną. Większość wniosków jest zatwierdzana w przeciągu kilku minut.
5. Jeśli zostaniesz poproszony o dostarczenie dodatkowych dokumentów, w ciągu 72 godzin dostaniesz email z instrukcjami.

(Source: Złóż wniosek o Elektroniczną Autoryzację Podróży (eTA), https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/visit-canada/eta/apply-pl.html)

To enter your Austrian passport number when applying for an eTA, follow these instructions:

- Enter the passport number that is at the top of the passport information page (the page with your photo).
- Most Austrian passport numbers are 8 characters long. They include 1 letter and 7 numbers. If the number you plan to enter is shorter or longer than this, check that you are using the right number.
- Passport numbers are made up of a combination of letters and numbers. Be extra careful with the letter O and the number 0, and the letter I and the number 1.
- Include any preceding characters.
- Remove any spaces.
- Don’t enter any special characters (like a hyphen).

To get a visitor visa to Canada, you must meet the following basic requirements:

- have a valid travel document, like a passport
- be in good health
- have no criminal or immigration-related convictions

- convince an immigration officer that you will leave Canada at the end of your visit
- have enough money for your stay (Source: Study permit: How to apply, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/study-permit/apply.html)

To determine if you need a transit visa or an Electronic Travel Authorization (eTA) to transit through Canada, you should consider the following factors:

- The type of travel document you plan to travel with
- The country that issued your travel document
- Your nationality
- Your method of travel to Canada for this trip

For example, if you are from an eTA-required country and plan to transit through Canada by air, you will need an eTA. However, if you are transiting by train, bus, boat, or cruise ship, you do not need an eTA but must bring the right travel documents. US citizens and lawful permanent residents of the U.S. can transit through Canada without a visa by any method of travel (Source: Transit through Canada, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/visit-canada/transit.html).

Additionally, citizens from some visa-required countries may be eligible to apply for an eTA instead of a visa if they meet specific requirements, such as having held a Canadian visitor visa in the past 10 years or currently holding a valid US non-immigrant visa (Source: Electronic travel authorization (eTA): Citizens from some visa-required countries, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/visit-canada/eta/eligibility/eta-x.html).

To determine if you need a transit visa or an Electronic Travel Authorization (eTA) to transit through Canada, consider the following:

1. **If you are from an eTA-required country**: You need an eTA to transit through Canada by air. You don't need an eTA if you're transiting through Canada and you enter by train, bus, boat, or cruise ship. (Source: Transit through Canada, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/visit-canada/transit.html)

2. **If you are a citizen or permanent resident of the United States**: You can transit through Canada without a visa or eTA by air, car, bus, train, boat, or cruise ship. (Source: Transit through Canada, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/visit-canada/transit.html)

3. **If you are a citizen from some visa-required countries**: You may be eligible to apply for an eTA instead of a visa if you meet specific requirements, such as having held a Canadian visitor visa in the past 10 years or currently holding a valid US non-immigrant visa. (Source: Electronic travel authorization (eTA): Citizens from some visa-required countries, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/visit-canada/eta/eligibility/eta-x.html)

4. **If you already have a valid Canadian visa**: You don’t need an eTA to fly to Canada and should continue to travel with your visitor visa until it expires. (Source: Electronic travel authorization (eTA): Citizens from some visa-required countries, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/visit-canada/eta/eligibility/eta-x.html)

5. **If you are not eligible for an eTA**: You need a visa to transit through Canada by air. (Source: Electronic travel authorization (eTA): Citizens from some visa-required countries, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/visit-canada/eta/eligibility/eta-x.html)

The duration of your responsibility depends on who you sponsor:

- For parents and grandparents, the undertaking period is 20 years (10 years in Quebec). (Source: What it means to be a sponsor, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/family-sponsorship/sponsor-parents-grandparents/undertaking.html)

- For a dependent child 22 years of age and older, the undertaking period is 3 years. (Source: Sponsor your spouse, partner or child: What it means to be a sponsor, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/family-sponsorship/spouse-partner-children/undertaking.html)
- For a dependent child under 22 years of age, the undertaking period is 10 years or until the child becomes 25 years of age, whichever comes first. (Source: Sponsor your spouse, partner or child: What it means to be a sponsor, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/family-sponsorship/spouse-partner-children/undertaking.html)

To start the citizenship test after receiving an invitation, follow these steps:

1. Sign in to the online test only after you receive an invitation.
2. Use your application number and your unique client identifier (UCI) to sign in.
3. Read and accept the privacy notice, and the terms and conditions.
4. Select the “Email me the test link” button at the bottom of the page. We’ll send the link to the same email address that received the test invitation (the email on your citizenship application) or your representative’s email.
5. If you’re using a representative, you’ll have an option to send the link to your email instead of theirs.
6. It may take a few minutes for you or your representative to receive the test link.
7. The link expires after 15 minutes. If your link expires, sign in again to get a new test link.
8. If you sent yourself a test link multiple times, use the latest test link to sign in.
9. Re-enter your application number and UCI to confirm your identity. (Source: Citizenship test: Take the online test, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/test/online.html)

To apply for Canadian citizenship for a minor under section 5(2), you need to provide the following documents:

1. **Document Checklist**: Download and complete the document checklist (Cit 0008) (Source: Canadian citizenship for minor 5(2) : Forms and documents to apply on paper, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/adult-minor/how/minor-5-2-forms-documents.html).

3. **Identity Page of the Minor’s Passports and Travel Documents**: Include colour copies of the identity page in the minor’s passports or travel documents, which should have their name, photo, date of birth, place of birth, document number, issue date, and expiration date. If the minor’s passport or travel document was extended, include a copy of the pages with the extension stamp. If there’s no passport or travel document during the eligibility period, explain why in question 8c of the application form (Source: Canadian citizenship for minor 5(2) : Forms and documents to apply on paper, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/adult-minor/how/minor-5-2-forms-documents.html).

4. **Proof of Relationship**: As the minor’s parent or legal guardian, provide a copy of one of the following documents:
   - A birth certificate listing you as the parent
   - An adoption order
   - A document issued by a provincial or territorial court (proof that you have custody of the minor)
   - An order of permanent guardianship (Source: Canadian citizenship for minor 5(1) : Forms and documents to apply on paper, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/adult-minor/how/minor-5-1-forms-documents.html).

Based on the provided sources, here are some common mistakes to avoid when writing a resume for a job in Canada:

1. **Leaving out important details**: Ensure your resume includes your education, qualifications, work experience (main duties for each job), current job title, and the city and country where you currently live (Source: International Experience Canada: Submit your work permit application, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/iec/apply-work-permit.html).

2. **Including false information**: Make sure to answer all questions truthfully and completely. Providing false information or leaving out important details can lead to your application being refused and may affect your eligibility for entry to Canada in the future (Source: International Experience Canada: Submit your work permit application, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/iec/apply-work-permit.html).

3. **Leaving gaps in work history**: Do not leave any gaps in time in the work history and education history sections. Include all absences, periods of unemployment, travel dates, etc. (Source: International Experience Canada: Submit your work permit application, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/iec/apply-work-permit.html).

4. **Using special characters or accents**: Use English and French letters only. If your passport uses other special letters or characters, use the letter without the accent (Source: International Experience Canada: Create your IEC profile and get your invitation to apply, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/iec/become-candidate.html).

5. **Not including all work experience**: Include all paid and unpaid work in the work history section (Source: International Experience Canada: Submit your work permit application, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/iec/apply-work-permit.html).

The immigration programs managed through Express Entry are:

- Canadian Experience Class
- Federal Skilled Worker Program
- Federal Skilled Trades Program

(Source: Immigrate through Express Entry, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry.html)

To qualify for the Canadian Experience Class, you need at least 1 year (or 1,560 hours) of skilled work experience in Canada within the 3 years before you apply. This can be a combination of full-time or part-time work in 1 or more jobs. The work must be in a TEER category 0, 1, 2, or 3 job, and you must have been authorized to work in Canada during this time. (Source: Express Entry: Canadian Experience Class, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/who-can-apply/canadian-experience-class.html)

The Federal Skilled Worker Program requires a minimum Canadian Language Benchmark (CLB) level of 7 in each of the four language abilities (speaking, listening, reading, and writing) for the first official language. For the second official language, you can get additional points if you have a score of at least CLB 5 in each of the four abilities. (Source: Express Entry: Federal Skilled Worker Program, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/express-entry/who-can-apply/federal-skilled-workers.html)

The main differences between an open work permit and an employer-specific work permit are:

1. **Employer-specific work permit**:
   - Lets you work in Canada under specific conditions, including the employer, location, and occupation (Source: Employer-specific work permits: eligibility, LMIA, and application steps, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/employer-specific.html).

2. **Open work permit**:
   - Lets you work for any employer in Canada, except those on the non-compliant list or those regularly offering specific adult services (Source: Open work permits: eligibility, restrictions, and application, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/open-work-permit.html).
   - You don’t need a job offer to apply, and the employer doesn’t need to apply for a Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) or pay the employer compliance fee (Source: Open work permits: eligibility, restrictions, and application, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/open-work-permit.html).

No, you don't need a job offer to apply for an open work permit. (Source: Open work permits: eligibility, restrictions, and application, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/open-work-permit.html)

A labour market impact assessment (LMIA) is a document that proves there’s a need to hire a foreign worker to fill the job. Most jobs need an LMIA. Your employer needs one unless the job is LMIA-exempt (Source: Employer-specific work permits: eligibility, LMIA, and application steps, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/employer-specific.html).

You must apply to restore your status no more than 90 days after your status expired. (Source: Restore your status and get a work permit, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/restore.html)

Yes, if you have an open work permit, you can change employers at any time while your work permit is valid. (Source: Extend or change the conditions on your work permit: Changing jobs or employers, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/extend/change-jobs-employers.html)

If you lose the job connected to your employer-specific work permit and want to continue working in Canada, you must get a new job offer and apply to change the conditions on your work permit. You must stop working for this or any other employer until your new work permit is approved or you receive a work authorization email (Source: Extend or change the conditions on your work permit: Changing jobs or employers, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/work-canada/extend/change-jobs-employers.html).

To be eligible to sponsor a spouse or common-law partner to Canada, you must meet the following criteria:

- You must be at least 18 years old.
- You must be a Canadian citizen, a permanent resident of Canada, or a person registered in Canada as an Indian under the Canadian Indian Act.
- You must not receive social assistance for reasons other than a disability.
- You must not be in prison, bankrupt, under a removal order, or charged with a serious crime.
- You must not have sponsored another spouse, common-law partner, or conjugal partner in the past, unless that person has become a Canadian citizen or has been a permanent resident of Canada for at least five years.
- You must promise to financially support your spouse or common-law partner and their dependent children (if applicable) and provide for their basic needs, such as food, shelter, and clothing, without needing social assistance from the government.

(Source: Sponsor your spouse, partner or children: Who you can sponsor, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/family-sponsorship/spouse-partner-children/who-you-can-sponsor.html)

In most cases, there isn’t an income requirement to sponsor your spouse (Source: Sponsor your spouse, partner or child: Check if you’re eligible, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/family-sponsorship/spouse-partner-children/eligibility.html).

No, the Parents and Grandparents Program is not accepting new sponsorship applications. The 2025 intake is closed and the last day to apply was October 9, 2025. (Source: Sponsor your parents and grandparents: How to apply, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/family-sponsorship/sponsor-parents-grandparents/apply.html)

If you can't sponsor your parents for permanent residence, they may be eligible to apply for a super visa which lets them stay in Canada for 5 years at a time. Parents and grandparents visiting on a super visa can also apply for 2-year extensions to their stay while they’re still in Canada. (Source: Sponsor your parents and grandparents, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/family-sponsorship/sponsor-parents-grandparents.html)

You may not be eligible to sponsor your spouse if you are receiving social assistance for a reason other than a disability. (Source: Sponsor your spouse, partner or child: Check if you’re eligible, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/immigrate-canada/family-sponsorship/spouse-partner-children/eligibility.html)

You must have been physically present in Canada for at least 1,095 days (3 years) during your 5-year eligibility period (Source: Canadian citizenship for adults and minor children: Who can apply, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/adult-minor/who.html).

Time spent in Canada as an international student before becoming a permanent resident can count towards citizenship, but only as half days, up to a maximum of 1 year (365 days). (Source: Changes to citizenship requirements 2017 to 2018, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/act-changes/requirements-2017-2018.html)

If you're between 18 to 54 years old, you must prove that you can speak and listen at the Canadian Language Benchmarks (CLB) Level 4 or higher in English or French. (Source: Find out if you have the language proof for citizenship: Step 1, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/become-canadian-citizen/eligibility/language-proof.html)

- Sign the Oath or Affirmation of Citizenship form (Source: Citizenship ceremony: What to expect at the ceremony, https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/canadian-citizenship/become-canadian-citizen/citizenship-ceremony/expect.html)
